query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A dual-framework predictive approach that separately models lattice vibrational and electronic heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr will predict each contribution to the total thermal conductivity within ±20% of experimental measurements, outperforming earlier methods that conflate these contributions using a single Debye temperature-based estimate.
generation.material_initial_state: Defect-free, single-phase HfNbTaTiZr alloy with controlled stoichiometry and minimal extrinsic defects (e.g., oxygen content ~1 wt.% for high-temperature samples).
generation.intervention: Implement a computational method combining on‐the‐fly machine-learned force fields to accurately capture lattice dynamics (phonon scattering due to local lattice distortions) and DFT-based electronic structure calculations to independently assess electron transport properties.
generation.conditions: The approach is applied at low temperatures (<200 K), where lattice and electronic contributions are comparable, and at high temperatures (300–1200 K) with controlled oxygen levels for consistency with reported experiments.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions modulating phonon scattering rates, quantified via effective interatomic force constants obtained from the machine-learned force field simulations.
generation.mechanism: By decoupling the simulation of phonon and electron transport, the model captures the distinct scattering processes induced by lattice disorder and electronic interactions, avoiding the oversimplifications of unified Debye temperature approaches.
generation.predicted_outcome: The predicted lattice and electronic contributions will match separated experimental conductivity measurements within ±20% across the tested temperature ranges, leading to a total thermal conductivity prediction closer to observed values than earlier unified methods.
generation.baseline: Existing analytical and simulation approaches that use a single Debye temperature estimate and fail to separately account for lattice distortions and electronic conduction in refractory high-entropy alloys.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to high-purity, single-phase HfNbTaTiZr alloys; performance may differ in specimens with significant microstructural defects, phase separations, or higher impurity levels.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty in the accuracy of the force field training and DFT approximations, particularly in the intermediate temperature range (~200–300 K) where the dominant transport mechanism transitions between lattice and electronic contributions.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate high-purity, defect-free samples of HfNbTaTiZr with controlled oxygen content. Perform separate experimental measurements of lattice and electronic thermal conductivities using techniques such as low-temperature calorimetry and frequency-domain thermoreflectance. Run simulations using the dual-framework approach to independently predict phonon and electron contributions across the temperature ranges (<200 K and 300–1200 K).
measurements: Lattice thermal conductivity (κ_l) via phonon-related calorimetry/analysis
Electronic thermal conductivity (κ_e) via carrier dynamics measurements (e.g., terahertz spectroscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the dual-framework predictions deviate by more than ±20% from experimental measurements for either the lattice or electronic contribution, or if the approach fails to distinctly reproduce the separate contributions observed at low (<200 K) and high (300–1200 K) temperatures, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The entropy of an HEA encompasses contributions that extend beyond the straightforward entropy of mixing, including vibrational, electronic, and magnetic components (). We note that due to the differing atomic sizes of individual alloy components, the atoms in an HEA do not sit on ideal lattice sites (defined by the Bravais lattice and basis vectors). Hence, the variation in atomic size and deviation of atom locations from the ideal lattice in a random solid solution provides an additional contribution to the entropy, which we denote noncomposition entropy ΔSnc. (This noncomposition entropy is distinct from the entropy of mixing ΔSm.) In a single-component glassy system, ΔSnc is referred to as “configurational” or “information” entropy or “complexity” (). Random local lattice distortions (misfit) are responsible, in part, for the high strength of high entropy alloys (e.g. see Refs ()). Here, we focus on the thermodynamic implications of such random distortions. The effects of atomic-size-induced distortions on structure and properties are difficult to assess in real alloy systems since these are necessarily convoluted with variations in bonding between different types of atoms ().

cited_evidence.text: In summary, this study has established a conductivity model for the HEA system Nb-Mo-Ta-W, designed alloy compositions with high conductivity and wear resistance, which can be applied to enhance the atomic-level resolution and lifespan of atomic force microscope probes. By adjusting the composition, a refractory high-entropy material of Nb15Mo35Ta15W35 was endowed with both high hardness and electrical conductivity. We indicate that the conductivity of Nb-Mo-Ta-W HEAs can be modulated through the cocktail effect but tends to differ by an order of magnitude compared to linear combinations. The reasons for the decrease in conductivity are attributed to changes in the plasma frequency and relaxation time resulting from lattice distortions, alterations in the effective mass and density of free electrons, and variations in the crystalline size after the formation of HEAs.

Figure 3 shows the temperature dependence of the measured κ, and the derived values of κe and κg for NiCoFeCrMn and NiCoFeCrPd. One distinct feature of the concentrated alloys, relative to pure metals, is that in a pure metal the total thermal conductivity is dominated by κe, and κg is usually negligible. However, in concentrated alloys, κg seems to dominate at low temperatures and is comparable with κe at about room temperature. Chemical disorder appears to scatter electrons more effectively than phonons. In addition, in pure metals κ starts decreasing at a few tens of K, while in concentrated alloys κ keeps increasing up to at least 300 K (see Table 3). One major reason is that, due to the large and nearly constant resistivity of these complex alloys, κe almost linearly increases with temperature up to 300 K, which is very different from the behavior in pure metals. The theoretical description of the temperature dependence of κg for disordered alloys has been challenging. However, numerical calculations of κg in equiatomic binary alloys of NiPd and NiPt show a very similar temperature dependence to what is shown in Fig. 3: at low temperature, κg increases rapidly with temperature
